This relatively brief embryonic phase is characteristic of precocial chicks that must rapidly achieve thermoregulatory independence, though the Green-legged partridge exhibits a slightly more extended developmental trajectory than some congeners. During the final days of incubation, the yolk-dependent embryo exhausts the albumen reserves and undergoes the critical transition to an exotrophic state, marked by the onset of pulmonary respiration and the absorption of the remaining yolk sac prior to pipping.

The downy chick progresses through distinct developmental stages, initially relying entirely on parental provisioning before gradually transitioning to independent foraging during the late nestling phase. The fledgling then enters a post-fledging dispersal phase, though it may remain within the natal territory for several additional days while refining its foraging skills under intermittent parental supervision.

Puberty, characterized by the onset of gonadal activity and the initiation of gametogenesis, is attained at 54 days after hatching [tp = 54 days after hatching] when birds are maintained at a stable ambient temperature of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C]. This relatively rapid attainment of reproductive capacity is notable among phasianids, reflecting a life-history strategy that prioritizes early breeding opportunities in the species' seasonally productive Southeast Asian forest habitats. The onset of puberty precedes first reproduction by a considerable margin, however, as young birds require additional time to establish territories and secure adequate body condition. During this pre-reproductive juvenile phase, immature individuals continue to refine their foraging efficiency and social interactions while undergoing the final stages of skeletal growth and plumage maturation. The subadult bird thus represents a critical transitional stage during which the energetic demands of growth gradually give way to the physiological preparations for breeding.

This mass difference likely reflects the energetic demands of male territorial defense and the physiological costs associated with female egg production. Comparative data from related species in the genera Arborophila and Tropicoperdix suggest that the Green-legged partridge occupies an intermediate position along the body size continuum within its clade. The species' relatively low metabolic rate, combined with its moderate adult body mass and extended lifespan, positions it as a slow-lived strategist within the broader context of tropical forest galliforms.
